procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 18, 1963, in Miscellaneous Petition No. 267 of 1962, dismissing the appellant's petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh seeking to quash an order and direct the government to treat his absence from duty as a period spent on duty and revise his pension. The High Court dismissed the petition but granted a certificate to file an appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed his petition. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the competent authority to reconsider the question after giving the appellant a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The respondent was ordered to pay the appellant's costs for both the Supreme Court appeal and the High Court petition.

directions: The High Court's order is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the competent authority has a duty under Fundamental Rule 54 to provide a government servant with an opportunity to show cause before forming an opinion on whether they were fully exonerated or their suspension was wholly unjustified, prior to making an order regarding their pay and allowances for the period of absence.

law.law_text: A decision-making process is considered an objective function, rather than a subjective one, when it depends on an examination of all facts and circumstances, involves arriving at factual findings, and can result in pecuniary loss to an individual.
When a function is objective in nature and affects an individual's rights, it implies a duty to act judicially.
A duty to act judicially requires adherence to the principles of natural justice, which include the right to be heard (i.e., an opportunity to show cause) before an adverse order is passed.

application.application_text: The Court analyzed the function of the competent authority under Fundamental Rule 54. It found that the authority must form an opinion on two factual questions: whether the government servant was 'fully exonerated' and whether their suspension was 'wholly unjustified'.

This process requires an examination of the 'facts and circumstances in their entirety.' Furthermore, an adverse order under this rule results in 'pecuniary loss to the government servant.' The Court, therefore, classified this function as objective rather than subjective.

The Court rejected the argument that an order under F.R. 54 is merely a 'consequential order' that doesn't require a new hearing. It pointed out that in some cases, no prior departmental inquiry is held, meaning the authority would not have the employee's side of the story.

Because the function is objective and carries significant financial consequences for the employee, the Court held that 'the very nature of the function implies the duty to act judicially.' This implied duty requires the application of the principles of natural justice.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the competent authority has an implied duty, based on the principles of natural justice, to provide a government servant with an opportunity to show cause before passing an order under F.R. 54. The Court reasoned that the decision is an objective function based on factual findings that can lead to pecuniary loss, which necessitates a fair hearing, even if the rule does not explicitly state so.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the competent authority has a duty under Fundamental Rule 54 to provide a government servant with an opportunity to show cause before forming an opinion on whether they were fully exonerated or their suspension was wholly unjustified, prior to making an order regarding their pay and allowances for the period of absence.
appellant_arguments: Before passing the impugned order under F.R. 54, the appellant ought to have been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action proposed.
The failure to provide such an opportunity renders the order invalid.
respondent_arguments: F.R. 54 does not explicitly or implicitly impose a duty on the authority to give an opportunity to show cause.
The order under F.R. 54 is merely a consequential order, following a departmental inquiry where an opportunity to show cause was already provided.
The only duty under F.R. 54 is for the government to consider whether the appellant was fully exonerated and if the suspension was wholly unjustified.
Once the authority formed the opinion that the suspension was not wholly unjustified, the relevant clauses of F.R. 54 applied, and the resulting order cannot be challenged.

cases.case_name: State of Orissa v. Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei
cases.principle: An order by the State to the prejudice of a person, in derogation of their vested rights, may be made only in accordance with the basic rules of justice and fair play, which requires giving the person an opportunity to set up their version or defense and to correct or controvert any evidence sought to be relied upon to their prejudice.

cases.case_name: V. K. Nambudiri v. Union of India
cases.principle: Where the nature of a function implies a duty to act judicially, an order is liable to be struck down as invalid if an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action is not afforded, as it would be in breach of the principles of natural justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a statutory rule requires an authority to make a decision based on an objective assessment of facts and circumstances, and that decision can result in adverse pecuniary consequences for a person, the function is considered judicial in nature. This imposes an implied duty on the authority to act in accordance with the principles of natural justice and provide the affected person with an opportunity to show cause before the adverse order is made, even if the rule does not explicitly state so. An order made in breach of this duty is invalid.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An order under Fundamental Rule 54, which determines a government servant's pay and allowances for a period of suspension and can result in significant pecuniary loss, is not a subjective or merely consequential decision. Instead, it is an objective function based on factual findings derived from the entirety of the case's facts and circumstances. The very nature of this function, which prejudices a person's vested rights, implies a duty to act judicially and in accordance with the principles of natural justice. Therefore, even though not explicitly stated in the rule, the authority has an implied duty to afford the government servant a reasonable opportunity to show cause before forming an opinion and passing an order under F.R. 54.
legal_tests_applied: The primary legal standard is whether the function performed by the authority is quasi-judicial in nature, thereby attracting the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem). The court determines this by assessing if the authority's decision is (1) objective rather than subjective, (2) based on an inquiry into facts and circumstances, and (3) results in adverse civil consequences (like pecuniary loss) for the individual. If these conditions are met, a duty to provide an opportunity to be heard is implied.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the respondent's argument that the order under F.R. 54 is merely a consequential order following a departmental inquiry. The court held that the fact an order is consequential does not determine whether an opportunity to show cause must be given.

The court further reasoned that an order under F.R. 54 is not always a consequential order, citing cases under Article 311 where no departmental inquiry is held (e.g., conviction on a criminal charge). In such instances, the authority would only have an ex-parte version of the facts, making a hearing essential to ensure fairness.
why_respondent_won: The court found that the decision-making process under F.R. 54 is an objective, not subjective, function. It requires the authority to examine all facts and circumstances to arrive at factual findings on whether the employee was fully exonerated and the suspension was wholly unjustified.
Because an order under F.R. 54 can result in pecuniary loss to the government servant, it adversely affects their vested rights.
The court held that the very nature of this objective, rights-affecting function implies a duty to act judicially.

This duty to act judicially requires adherence to the principles of natural justice, which includes affording the affected person a reasonable opportunity to show cause before an adverse order is made.
policy_considerations: An order by the State to the prejudice of a person in derogation of his vested rights may be made only in accordance with the basic rules of justice and fairplay.

The deciding authority is under a duty to give the person against whom an enquiry is held an opportunity to set up his version or defence and an opportunity to correct or to controvert any evidence in the possession of the authority which is sought to be relied upon to his prejudice.
F.R. 54 contemplates a duty to act in accordance with the basic concept of justice and fairplay.
